aspects.says: Platform threads in a pool sized to the cores stay the right choice for CPU-bound work.
aspects.reason: asked in the sibling page's quiz (6.7.1, the CPU-bound question); a speed-up test is not allowed

aspects.says: A virtual thread is always a daemon at NORM_PRIORITY, so a thread that must be non-daemon or needs a priority is a platform thread.
basis: section:6.7.2.3. Compatibility with Existing Code and Libraries

aspects.says: Java 24 (JEP 491) removes pinning in synchronized, but on Java 21 it is still a concern.
aspects.reason: a version fact; the quiz's pinning question is set on Java 21, which is what the course runs

aspects.says: JFR recordings and jcmd JSON thread dumps show virtual threads in production.
aspects.reason: tools run from outside the program, with nothing a practice can grade; the monitor practice covers the naming and counting side

aspects.says: java.util.concurrent tools such as BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch and ExecutorService work unchanged on virtual threads, and a virtual thread waiting in take() unmounts.
Migrating replaces a fixed pool with a per-task executor, synchronized with ReentrantLock where it blocks, and adds a Semaphore in front of a scarce resource.
aspects.reason: each step is practised on its own: the per-task executor and the semaphore by the sibling page's fanout and throttle practices, the lock choice by this page's cache practice

aspects.says: sleep(0) yields a virtual thread, a thread joining itself waits forever without a timeout, and InheritableThreadLocal values pass to child virtual threads.
aspects.reason: minor behaviours the page lists in passing, each a one-line fact with nothing further to practise

aspects.says: Thread.getAllStackTraces() leaves virtual threads out, so they are named through a builder factory and watched with tools that see them.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: A virtual thread is also pinned while it runs a native method through JNI.
basis: section:6.7.2.3. Compatibility with Existing Code and Libraries
aspects.reason: a minor fact with nothing to write in a Java-only practice; the pinning question covers what pinning costs

aspects.says: Virtual threads improve throughput, not the latency of a single task, and a benchmark needs thousands of I/O-bound tasks to show it.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: a performance claim that only a timing benchmark could show, and timing tests are not deterministic; the sibling page's quiz asks the same idea

aspects.says: On Java 21 a virtual thread that blocks inside synchronized pins its carrier, and the scheduler adds no carrier to make up for it.
Code that blocks while holding a lock uses a ReentrantLock unlocked in finally rather than synchronized, so a waiting virtual thread parks instead of pinning.
A virtual thread starts at a few hundred bytes and maps many-to-few onto carriers, so millions fit where platform threads stop at thousands.
aspects.reason: a memory and scale claim no test can measure deterministically on a shared runner; the sibling page's fanout practice keeps many virtual threads in flight at once

aspects.says: The scheduler is a work-stealing ForkJoinPool whose parallelism and maxPoolSize are set by system properties, and a resumed virtual thread may land on another carrier.
aspects.reason: an implementation detail set by JVM flags that a graded test cannot control or observe reliably

aspects.says: -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads and the JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event find pinning during development.
A blocked platform thread holds its OS thread, while a blocked virtual thread unmounts and frees its carrier.
aspects.reason: which carrier runs a virtual thread is up to the scheduler, so no test can observe unmounting deterministically; it is asked in the sibling page's quiz (6.7.1, the carrier question)

aspects.says: Virtual threads always belong to the VirtualThreads thread group, which cannot be chosen.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
